name: Mirror checking / mirror avoidance

lead: Mirror checking means repeatedly inspecting your appearance; mirror avoidance means steering clear of mirrors altogether. Both are described in body dysmorphic disorder, and knowing them helps people spot when self-monitoring has become a habit that feeds fixation rather than helping them look better.

In BDD they are treated as rituals that maintain preoccupation, and CBT with exposure and response prevention targets them directly. Sources on how these habits show up in looksmaxxing communities specifically are thin; most research sits in the BDD literature.

paras: In practice people notice how often they check, how long they spend and what they feel afterwards, or how much they avoid reflective surfaces. In therapy, exposure and response prevention involves gradually cutting back checking or approaching avoided mirrors under guidance.

In BDD both patterns are described as time-consuming and linked to distress, and clinicians assess them as part of diagnosis. People who find them hard to control can speak with a doctor or mental health professional.

angle.text: Forum users describe mirror checking and avoidance as habits that keep attention on perceived flaws and warp self-image. Cutting them back is a target of CBT, with the aim of a steadier, more relaxed relationship with your own appearance.

lead: Mirror checking and mirror avoidance are two opposite behavioral patterns around reflective surfaces that are described in body dysmorphic disorder (BDD). Wikipedia lists repetitive checking of one's appearance as a characteristic behavior of BDD and notes that some people instead avoid mirrors.[1]

In looksmaxxing communities the terms describe self-monitoring habits tied to appearance anxiety. Research on them is mainly within the BDD literature, where exposure and response prevention targets such rituals.
infobox: Exposure and response prevention within CBT

paras: Wikipedia describes mirror checking as one of several repetitive behaviors in BDD, alongside reassurance seeking, comparing with others, camouflaging with clothing or cosmetics, excessive grooming and skin picking.[1] The same article says some people with BDD avoid mirrors instead.[1]
People with BDD may spend several hours a day or more preoccupied with the perceived flaw.[1]

No studies found specific to mirror checking or avoidance in looksmaxxing communities. Cognitive-behavioral treatment for BDD, which includes exposure with response prevention aimed at rituals such as checking, has been studied in randomized trials more broadly; see CBT for BDD.
